lessons.title: An Inspector Calls: plot and structure
lessons.summary: Follow the events of Priestley's play act by act, then learn how its tight three-act structure, cliffhangers and twist ending are built to deliver a message.
objectives: I can retell the main events of An Inspector Calls in the correct order.
I can explain each character's part in the chain of events that led to Eva Smith's death.
I can describe the play's structure: three acts in real time, cliffhangers and a cyclical ending.
I can explain how Priestley uses structure to control tension and deliver his message.

activities.title: Act One: the celebration interrupted
activities.content:
## Act One

The play opens in spring 1912, in the comfortable dining room of the **Birling** family in the industrial town of Brumley. **Arthur Birling**, a wealthy factory owner, is celebrating the engagement of his daughter **Sheila** to **Gerald Croft**, son of a rival businessman. Also present are his wife **Sybil** and son **Eric**, who is already drinking heavily.

Birling makes a series of confident speeches. He predicts there will be no war, describes a new ocean liner as unsinkable, and tells the young men that everyone should look after himself and his own. As he says this, the doorbell rings.

**Inspector Goole** enters and announces that a young woman, **Eva Smith**, has died in the infirmary after drinking disinfectant. He shows a photograph to Birling, who admits he sacked her from his factory two years earlier for leading a strike for higher wages. Birling insists this has nothing to do with her death.

The Inspector then turns to Sheila. She recognises the girl: in a jealous temper, she had her dismissed from a job at Milwards department store. Sheila is deeply upset. Finally the Inspector mentions that Eva changed her name to **Daisy Renton**. Gerald's reaction shows he knew her, and the act ends as the Inspector re-enters and asks, simply, *Well?*

activities.title: Using a plot event as evidence
activities.content:
In the exam, retelling the story earns almost nothing. Each event should be used as **evidence** for a point about character, theme or method.

| Plot event | Weak (retelling) | Strong (using the event) |
|---|---|---|
| The doorbell rings during Birling's speech | "Then the doorbell rings and the Inspector comes in." | "Priestley times the doorbell to cut off Birling in the middle of preaching self-interest, so the Inspector's arrival physically interrupts the idea that everyone should look after himself." |
| Sheila had Eva sacked from Milwards | "Sheila got Eva sacked because she was jealous." | "Sheila's confession that she used her family's power to punish a shop-girl for a moment of jealousy shows how casual cruelty from the wealthy can start a chain of harm." |

The strong versions say **what Priestley does**, use a **precise detail**, and explain **why it matters**.

question.text: Put these events from Act One in the order they happen.
question.hint: The Inspector arrives during Birling's speech, and Birling is questioned before Sheila.
question.explanation: The dinner and engagement come first, then Birling's speeches, then the doorbell and the Inspector's arrival. Birling admits sacking Eva, then Sheila admits her part, and the act ends with the name Daisy Renton and Gerald's reaction.
order: The Birlings celebrate Sheila's engagement to Gerald
Birling tells Gerald and Eric that a man should look after himself
The doorbell rings and Inspector Goole is shown in
Birling admits he sacked Eva Smith after a strike
Sheila admits she had Eva dismissed from Milwards
The Inspector reveals Eva used the name Daisy Renton

activities.title: Act Two: Gerald and Mrs Birling
activities.content:
## Act Two

Act Two begins exactly where Act One stopped. Under pressure, **Gerald** admits that the previous summer he met Daisy Renton in the Palace bar, rescued her from an unpleasant older man, and installed her in a friend's empty flat. She became his mistress for several months before he ended it. Sheila, though hurt, respects his honesty and hands back the engagement ring.

**Mrs Birling** enters, confident that the Inspector cannot touch her. She learns that Eva, now pregnant and destitute, came to the charity committee Mrs Birling chairs, using the name *Mrs Birling*. Offended, Sybil used her influence to refuse the girl help. She insists she did nothing wrong.

The Inspector asks who the father of the child was. Mrs Birling, not realising the truth, declares that the young man responsible should be made an example of and take full responsibility. Sheila desperately tries to stop her. Then the front door slams: **Eric** is back. The act ends as everyone looks at him, and the audience understands what Mrs Birling has just done.

This act is a masterclass in **dramatic irony**: the audience works out the truth about Eric before Mrs Birling does, so every proud sentence she speaks tightens the trap around her own son.

question.text: Why is the end of Act Two so powerful for the audience?
question.hint: Think about what Mrs Birling has just said about the father of Eva's child, and who walks in.
question.explanation: Mrs Birling has insisted the father of the child should be publicly blamed and punished, without realising the father is her own son. When Eric enters, the audience sees her words turn against her. This is dramatic irony combined with a cliffhanger.

options.text: Mrs Birling has demanded the father be punished, and the audience realises the father is Eric just as he enters
The Inspector arrests Gerald for his affair with Daisy Renton
options.feedback: No one is arrested; the Inspector is not interested in legal punishment.

options.text: Sheila reveals that she was the one who found Eva's body
Birling confesses that he knew Eva was pregnant

activities.title: Act Three: confession, speech and twist
activities.content:
## Act Three

**Eric** confesses. He met Eva in the Palace bar, forced his way into her lodgings while drunk, and later learnt she was pregnant. He stole money from his father's office to support her, but she refused it once she knew it was stolen. When Eric realises his mother turned Eva away, he turns on her in fury.

The **Inspector** then delivers his final speech. He reminds them that there are millions of Eva Smiths, that people are responsible for each other, and that if they refuse to learn the lesson they will be taught it in fire, blood and anguish. He leaves.

Now the play twists. Gerald returns having spoken to a policeman: there is no Inspector Goole on the force. Birling telephones the Chief Constable to confirm it. Then Gerald rings the infirmary: no girl has died that night. The older Birlings and Gerald are jubilant, treating the evening as a hoax and a lucky escape. Sheila and Eric are appalled: whatever the Inspector was, they did those things.

The telephone rings. Birling answers. A girl has just died on her way to the infirmary, and a police inspector is on his way to ask questions. The curtain falls on their frozen faces.

The ending sends the play back to its beginning, a **cyclical structure**, and leaves the audience to decide what the Inspector was and whether the family will change.

question.hint: Think in order: factory, shop, Palace bar (twice), charity committee.
question.explanation: Birling sacked her from his factory. Sheila had her dismissed from Milwards. Gerald made her his mistress and then left her. Eric got her pregnant and stole money to help her. Mrs Birling refused her charity help.

Had her dismissed from Milwards after a jealous complaint
Kept her as his mistress for a few months, then ended it
Got her pregnant and stole money to try to support her
Used her influence to refuse her help from the charity committee

activities.title: The structure of the play
activities.content:
## A tightly built machine

Priestley designed the play so that every part supports the message. Key structural features:

**Three acts, one room, real time.** The whole play happens in one evening in one dining room, with no gaps in time between acts. This follows the classical **unities** of time, place and action. Nothing distracts from the interrogation, and the audience feels trapped alongside the Birlings.

**A chain of confessions.** The Inspector works through the family one at a time, always in the same order of moral awareness: Birling (denial), Sheila (guilt), Gerald (shame), Mrs Birling (denial), Eric (despair). Each story adds a link to the chain.

**Cliffhangers.** Act One ends on Gerald's guilty face; Act Two ends on Eric's entrance. Priestley leaves the audience in suspense at each curtain, and each act opens exactly where the last stopped, so the pressure never releases.

**The well-made play, subverted.** Traditional 'well-made plays' end with every question answered. Priestley uses the same tools (a secret from the past, a mounting crisis, a final revelation) but refuses the tidy ending. The final phone call reopens everything.

**Cyclical structure.** The play ends with an inspector about to arrive, just as it began. The Birlings are given a second chance, and so is the audience.

**Dramatic irony.** Because the play is set in 1912 but was first performed in 1945, the audience knows Birling's confident predictions are wrong. Structure and context work together to undermine him from the start.

activities.title: Writing about structure
activities.content:
**Question:** How does Priestley use the ending of the play to convey his ideas?

> Priestley's ending is deliberately unresolved. After the Inspector leaves, the family discovers he was not a real police officer and that no girl has died, and the play seems to be heading towards the comfortable resolution of a well-made play. Birling and Mrs Birling relax, and Gerald offers Sheila the ring again. Then the telephone rings with news of a real death and a real inspector on his way. By returning the family to the moment before the first doorbell, Priestley creates a cyclical structure that suggests the lesson has not been learnt and must be repeated. The audience, unlike Birling, has watched the whole evening and knows what is coming, so the final curtain challenges them to ask whether they, too, would need to be taught twice.

**Why it works:** it names structural features (unresolved ending, well-made play, cyclical structure), refers to exact moments, and links the structure to Priestley's purpose and the audience's response.

question.text: True or false: each act of An Inspector Calls begins exactly where the previous act ended, so no stage time passes between acts.
question.hint: Think about the first lines of Act Two and Act Three.
question.explanation: True. The play runs in continuous real time in a single room. This creates a sense of pressure and inescapability, and follows the classical unities of time, place and action.

options.text: True
False

question.text: Complete the sentences about the structure of the play.

metadata.blanksText: The play is set in 1912 but was first performed in 1945, so the audience knows Birling's predictions are wrong; this is ___ irony. Act One and Act Two both end on a ___ that keeps the audience in suspense. The final phone call returns the family to where they started, creating a ___ structure.

question.hint: The audience knows more than the character; a suspenseful act ending; a shape that goes round in a circle.
question.explanation: Dramatic irony arises when the audience knows what the characters do not. Both acts end on a cliffhanger. The ending is cyclical because it takes the family back to the start.

question.text: Explain why Priestley has the Inspector question the characters one at a time rather than all together, and what effect this has on the audience.
question.hint: Think about the chain of events, the build-up of tension, and how each confession makes the next one harder to deny.
question.explanation: Questioning one at a time lets the story of Eva's life unfold in chronological order, so the audience sees each act of selfishness as a link in a chain. It builds tension, as each character waits for their turn and the audience guesses who is next. It also allows Priestley to contrast responses: the young accept blame, the old deny it. Each confession makes the family's collective responsibility harder to dismiss.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that the one-by-one method reveals Eva's story as a chain of events in chronological order
Explains that it builds tension or suspense as the audience anticipates who is next
Comments on contrast between characters' responses or on building a sense of shared responsibility

question.text:
How does Priestley use the structure of An Inspector Calls to make the audience think about responsibility? Write about:

- how the play is organised into acts and how each act ends
- how the ending of the play affects the audience.
question.hint: Consider real time and one setting, the order of confessions, the cliffhangers at the end of Acts One and Two, the Inspector's exit speech, the false relief, and the final phone call.
question.explanation: A strong answer explains the single setting and continuous time as trapping the family and audience together; the chain of confessions building a picture of shared responsibility; the cliffhangers keeping tension high; the Inspector's speech placed just before the twist so its message lingers; the false relief exposing the older generation's refusal to learn; and the cyclical ending forcing the family, and the audience, to face the lesson again.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies the single setting and continuous real time as creating pressure or a sense of being trapped
Explains the chain of confessions as showing how each character contributed to Eva's death
Refers to a cliffhanger at the end of Act One or Act Two and its effect
Comments on the placing of the Inspector's final speech before his exit
Analyses the false relief or hoax section as exposing who has and has not learnt the lesson
Explains the final phone call or cyclical ending as forcing the audience to reflect on responsibility

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Act One**: engagement dinner, Birling's confident speeches, the Inspector arrives; Birling and Sheila confess; Gerald reacts to *Daisy Renton*.
- **Act Two**: Gerald's affair; Sheila returns the ring; Mrs Birling refuses to accept blame and condemns the unknown father; Eric enters.
- **Act Three**: Eric's confession; the Inspector's final speech and exit; the family discovers he was not real; the final phone call.
- Chain of responsibility: **Birling → Sheila → Gerald → Mrs Birling → Eric**.
- Structure: **three acts in real time**, one room (**unities**), **cliffhangers**, a subverted **well-made play**, **dramatic irony**, and a **cyclical ending**.
- In essays, use events as **evidence** for points about character, theme and Priestley's purpose.

practiceQuestions.text: In which year is An Inspector Calls set?
practiceQuestions.hint: Birling talks about a famous liner that is about to sail.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The play is set in spring 1912, shortly before the Titanic sank and two years before the First World War, though it was written and first performed in 1945.

options.feedback: 1945 is when the play was written and first performed.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: the Inspector arrives at the very moment Birling is telling Eric and Gerald that a man should look after himself and his own.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the timing of the doorbell in Act One.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Priestley times the doorbell to interrupt Birling's speech about self-interest, so the Inspector's entrance seems to answer it directly.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Put these events from Act Three in the correct order.
practiceQuestions.hint: Eric's confession comes first; the final phone call is the last thing that happens.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Eric confesses, the Inspector gives his speech and leaves, Gerald returns with news that there is no Inspector Goole, the infirmary confirms no death, then the telephone rings with news of a real death.
order: Eric admits his part in Eva's story and confronts his mother
The Inspector delivers his final speech and leaves
Gerald returns and says there is no Inspector Goole on the police force
A call to the infirmary confirms that no girl has died that night

practiceQuestions.text: Under what name did Eva Smith approach Mrs Birling's charity committee?
practiceQuestions.hint: The name was the reason Mrs Birling felt insulted.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Eva called herself Mrs Birling, which offended Sybil Birling and led her to use her influence to refuse the girl help. Later it becomes clear why Eva may have chosen that name.

options.text: Mrs Birling
Daisy Renton
options.feedback: Daisy Renton was the name she used when she met Gerald.

options.text: Eva Croft
Sheila Smith

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentence about the setting.

metadata.blanksText: The whole play takes place in the ___ room of the Birlings' house in the industrial town of ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: The family is having a meal; the town's name begins with B.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The single setting is the Birlings' dining room in Brumley, a fictional industrial town in the North Midlands.

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO of the following are true about how each act ends?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what the audience is left looking at when the curtain falls on Acts One and Two.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Act One ends with Gerald's reaction to the name Daisy Renton and the Inspector's single-word question; Act Two ends with Eric's entrance after his mother has condemned the unknown father. The Inspector does not arrest anyone, and Sheila returns the ring in the middle of Act Two, not at its end.

options.text: Act One ends with Gerald exposed as having known Daisy Renton
Act Two ends with Eric entering just after Mrs Birling has blamed the unknown father
Act One ends with the Inspector arresting Birling
Act Two ends with Sheila handing back her engagement ring
options.feedback: Sheila returns the ring earlier in Act Two.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each structural term to its meaning.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about time, endings and what the audience knows.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The unities are the classical rules of one time, one place, one action. A cliffhanger is a suspenseful act ending. Dramatic irony is when the audience knows more than the characters.

pairs.right: One place, one continuous stretch of time, one main action
An act ending that leaves the audience in suspense
The audience knows something the characters do not

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why the discovery that Inspector Goole may not be a real police officer is important to the structure and meaning of the play.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how different characters react to the news, and what the final phone call then does.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The discovery creates a false resolution: the older Birlings and Gerald treat the evening as a hoax and feel relieved, while Sheila and Eric insist their actions were real regardless. This divides the generations and shows who has learnt the lesson. The final phone call then destroys the relief, suggesting the Inspector's identity matters less than the truth he revealed.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that the discovery creates a false sense of relief or resolution before the final twist
Contrasts the reactions of the older generation (and Gerald) with Sheila and Eric
Comments that the final phone call reverses the relief or that the Inspector's identity matters less than the family's actions

practiceQuestions.text: Which statement best explains why Priestley set the play in 1912 rather than 1945, when it was written?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about Birling's predictions and what the 1945 audience had lived through.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Setting the play in 1912 means the audience knows Birling's optimism about peace, prosperity and the unsinkable ship is wrong. This dramatic irony discredits him and his views from the start.

options.text: So the audience can see Birling's confident predictions proved wrong by history, discrediting his views
Because police inspectors did not exist in 1945
Because Priestley wanted to write a historical romance
Because the theatre could not afford modern costumes

practiceQuestions.text: How does Priestley use the ending of Act Two to create tension and to expose Mrs Birling? Refer to what happens on stage and to the structure of the scene.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about Mrs Birling's confidence, her demand that the father be punished, Sheila's attempts to stop her, the audience's growing realisation, and Eric's entrance as the curtain falls.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong answer explains that Mrs Birling's confidence makes her condemnation of the unknown father seem safe to her; that Sheila's interruptions signal to the audience what is coming; that dramatic irony builds as the audience realises Eric is the father before his mother does; that Priestley delays Eric's entrance to the last possible moment as a cliffhanger; and that the moment exposes Mrs Birling's hypocrisy and prepares the confrontation of Act Three.

markScheme.criterion: Refers to Mrs Birling's demand that the father of the child be held responsible or punished
Identifies dramatic irony: the audience realises Eric is the father before Mrs Birling does
Comments on Sheila's attempts to warn or stop her mother as increasing tension
Analyses Eric's entrance at the curtain as a cliffhanger
Explains what the moment exposes about Mrs Birling (hypocrisy, arrogance, refusal to accept responsibility)

practiceQuestions.text: Put these events from Act Two in the order in which they happen on stage.
practiceQuestions.hint: Gerald is dealt with before Mrs Birling, and Sheila's ring is returned before Gerald goes out.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Act Two moves from Gerald to Mrs Birling. Gerald confesses his affair, Sheila returns the ring, and Gerald leaves. The Inspector then turns to Mrs Birling, who admits refusing help to the girl and insists the father of the child must be dealt with severely. The act ends as Eric walks in.
order: Gerald admits that he met Daisy Renton at the Palace bar and kept her as his mistress
Sheila hands Gerald back the engagement ring
Gerald leaves the house to walk and think
Mrs Birling admits she refused the girl help from her charity committee
Mrs Birling insists the father of the child must be made to take responsibility
Eric enters and the curtain falls

practiceQuestions.text: Why does the end of Act One leave the audience in suspense?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how Gerald reacts when he hears a particular name, and how quickly the curtain falls after that.
practiceQuestions.explanation: When the Inspector says the girl changed her name to Daisy Renton, Gerald is visibly startled and admits to Sheila that he knew her. The Inspector re-enters, asks a single word, and the curtain falls before Gerald can explain. The audience must wait for Act Two to hear his story.

options.text: Gerald's startled reaction to the name Daisy Renton shows he knew her, but the act ends before he can explain
The Inspector announces that he is going to arrest Mr Birling for causing the girl's death
options.feedback: The Inspector never arrests anyone; he is interested in moral, not legal, guilt.

options.text: Sheila faints when she sees the photograph of the girl
Eric confesses that he stole money from his father's office
options.feedback: Eric's confession about the money comes in Act Three.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each place in Eva Smith's story to what happened to her there.
practiceQuestions.hint: Follow her life in order: a factory, a shop, a bar, a committee room, a hospital.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Eva was sacked from Birling's factory after the strike, then dismissed from Milwards after Sheila complained. She met Gerald, and later Eric, at the Palace bar. Mrs Birling's committee turned her away when she asked for help, and she died in the infirmary after drinking disinfectant.

pairs.right: Sacked for leading a demand for higher wages
Dismissed after a customer complained about her
Met Gerald, and later Eric, while alone and short of money
Refused help when she asked for it while pregnant

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: the action of An Inspector Calls moves between several locations, including Milwards and the Palace bar, so the audience sees the events of Eva's life directly on stage.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about where every scene of the play takes place, and how the audience learns about Eva.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The whole play takes place in one room, the Birlings' dining room, and in one continuous stretch of time. Eva never appears on stage; the audience learns her story only through the characters' confessions and the Inspector's account.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about how Priestley organises the play.

metadata.blanksText: The play uses a ___ setting, the Birlings' dining room, which the characters cannot escape. The Inspector questions the family in the ___ order of Eva's life, so her story unfolds step by step. The play closes with a final ___ when the telephone rings to announce that a real inspector is on his way.

practiceQuestions.hint: One place only; the order in which things happened in time; an unexpected turn at the very end.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Priestley keeps to a single setting to trap the family and the audience together. The questioning follows the chronological order of Eva's life, from the factory to the charity committee. The final phone call is a twist that snatches away the family's relief.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why Priestley places the Inspector's final speech immediately before the family begin to doubt whether he was a real police officer, and what effect this order of events has on the audience.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what the audience is left remembering, what the doubt then tests in each character, and whether the message depends on who delivered it.
practiceQuestions.explanation: By placing the speech before any doubt is raised, Priestley lets its warning about shared responsibility land with full authority and linger in the audience's mind. The doubt that follows then acts as a test: Sheila and Eric hold on to the lesson, while the older Birlings and Gerald use the doubt to escape it. The audience is pushed to see that the message is true whether or not the Inspector was real.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that the speech is delivered before doubt so its message carries full weight and stays with the audience
Explains that the doubt then tests the characters and reveals who has learnt the lesson
Comments that the audience realises the message is true regardless of whether the Inspector was real

practiceQuestions.text:
How does Priestley use the opening of the play, before the Inspector arrives, to prepare the audience for what follows? Write about:

- the mood of the celebration and how the family behave
- how Birling's speeches and the Inspector's arrival are arranged.
practiceQuestions.hint: Consider the comfortable, self-satisfied atmosphere; the lighting change described in the stage directions; Birling's confident predictions; the timing of the doorbell; and the small cracks in the family's happiness, such as Eric's behaviour and Sheila's teasing of Gerald.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong answer shows that Priestley builds a comfortable, complacent mood of celebration so that its collapse is more powerful; that the stage direction changing the lighting from soft and warm to hard and bright signals the shift from comfort to interrogation; that Birling's predictions create dramatic irony which undermines his authority before the Inspector even speaks; that the doorbell cuts across Birling's speech about every man looking after himself, so the Inspector arrives as a direct answer to that view; that small cracks such as Eric's nervousness and Sheila's remarks about last summer foreshadow the confessions; and that the whole opening sets up a fall from celebration to exposure.

markScheme.criterion: Describes the comfortable, self-satisfied mood of the engagement celebration and its purpose in setting up a fall
Refers to the lighting change in the stage directions as marking a shift in mood
Explains Birling's confident predictions as dramatic irony that undermines him
Comments on the timing of the doorbell interrupting Birling's speech about self-reliance
Identifies hints of tension or foreshadowing in the family before the Inspector arrives
Explains how the opening contrasts with, or prepares for, the exposure and collapse that follows
